description.narrative: Sierra Leone remains one of the least developed nations in the world, with a UN HDI rating of 174/178 (HDI, 2013). The vast majority of economic activity in Sierra Leone is informal, with the formal sector dominated by large-scale mining. More than two-thirds of the population rely on agriculture for their livelihoods, mostly in subsistence farming, with rice as the staple crop and cassava been the major substitute. Agricultural production accounts for 45-50% of total GDP. Cassava been second most important food crop in Sierra Leone after rice and constituting a significant portion of the diet of the rural populations in every part of the country has over the years been grossly under developed. Cassava processing has been more of ‘boil and eat’ while marketing had been with wide price fluctuation within seasons and locations. However, efforts to develop cassava sector had always been geared towards fight against mosaic diseases to improve production, which is just one aspect of the value chain while other aspects have received inadequate attention thus limiting intervention impacts. The Adding value to cassava through improved processing and marketing of the product (‘‘Cassava Biznes na Salon’’) project is in line with objectives expressed in the Government of Sierra Leone’s policy framework for agricultural development and guided by the National Agricultural Investment Plan (NAIP), which proposes to reduce poverty and food insecurity (MDG1) and thus contribute in achieving the MDG by 2015. The Sierra Leone Agenda for prosperity highlights agricultural development as the pathway to sustainable economic growth for the country. The Government’s flagship Smallholder Commercialization Programme (SCP) is a major component of the National Sustainable Agriculture Development Programme (2010-2030) and has processing and value addition as one of its main thrust.
